title: Rebuild the machine from labelled switches
allegory: A transcoder is like rebuilding a sealed factory machine as a glass one made of labelled switches: the same materials go in, nearly the same product comes out, and you can see which few switches flipped and trace them to the machines upstream.
map: the MLP layer, dense and in superposition
the materials fed in and the product that comes out
ln(resid_mid) going in, mlp_out coming out
a few labelled switches flipping on, each adding its own part
sparse latents: encoder and ReLU, each adding its decoder vector
tracing which upstream switches flip this one
the pullback W_decᵀ f_later: influence from weights alone
a photo of the product vs a rebuilt machine
an SAE reconstructs an activation; a transcoder replaces the computation

cap.1: You can photograph what goes into a machine and what comes out, but the machine itself is sealed. You still cannot say what it did.
cap.2: An SAE is a debugger breakpoint: it reads the variables at one point. MLP neurons are in superposition, so staring at the layer's weights does not tell you what it computes.
cap.3: SAEs decompose state at a hook point, not the function between points. MLP latents are spread across neurons in superposition, so the layer's function does not decompose by neuron.

cap.1: Rebuild it as a glass machine made of labelled switches. Same materials in, nearly the same product out, and you can see which few switches flipped.
cap.2: A transcoder is SAE-shaped, but it takes the MLP's input and learns to produce the MLP's output through a sparse layer of latents. It swaps the subroutine for a readable one.
cap.3: Transcoder: ln(resid_mid) → sparse latents → mlp_out. Strictly a mapping, not an autoencoder; evidence so far suggests no Pareto penalty against SAEs for the gain in readability.

cap.1: Each switch watches the input for one pattern. The few that fire each add their own fixed part, and the parts sum to the output.
cap.2: Same shapes as an SAE: encoder, ReLU, sparse code, decoder. Only the target changes: the decoder must produce mlp_out from ln(resid_mid), not rebuild its own input.
cap.3: f = ReLU(W_enc x + b_enc), mlp_out ≈ W_dec f + b_dec, trained on (input, output) pairs with a sparsity penalty, so the layer's function splits into sparse, independently varying units.

cap.1: Because every switch is a fixed pattern, you can ask which earlier switches would flip this one straight from the wiring, before reading any text.
cap.2: Pullback: dot the later latent's encoder direction with each earlier transcoder's decoder directions to rank upstream latents. Against the embedding it gives the driving tokens.
cap.3: p = W_decᵀ f_later ranks upstream latents from weights alone; times their activations it gives input-dependent influence. ARENA's layer-8 latent traces mostly to head 8.5 and MLP7.

chapters.verdict: De-embed against what the layer actually reads.

cap.1: Ask which words flip a switch using the raw word list and you get noise: an early layer rewrites every word before this machine ever sees it.
cap.2: In GPT-2, MLP0 acts as an extended embedding and rewrites each token first. De-embed against W_E plus MLP0's output (create_extended_embedding), then cross-check with pullbacks.
cap.3: Naive W_E @ f_later asks what the latent reads from a representation the model never has. Normalise(W_E + MLP0(ln2(W_E))) usually resolves the token list; including MLP0 matters most.

cap.1: You can keep the old machine running and just watch the glass one, or truly swap it in and see whether the factory still works.
cap.2: use_error_term=True keeps the model's real MLP output and only caches transcoder activations. False substitutes the transcoder's output for mlp_out, which is what replacement hooks do.
cap.3: With the error term the model's behaviour is unchanged and latents explain the non-error part; without it you run the replacement model, whose fidelity bounds every conclusion.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Read what a layer does, not just holds
Trace causes from the wiring first
The building block of attribution graphs

cap.1: To understand a model you need to know what its parts do, not just what they hold. Transcoders turn a sealed layer into steps you can read and trace.
cap.2: Attribution graphs are built from transcoders: you cannot trace a computation through MLPs you cannot decompose. Weights-first theories, checked on text, are the habit to keep.
cap.3: Sparse, readable replacements for MLPs make circuits through MLPs tractable: the basis for attribution graphs and for hypotheses formed from weights, then tested on activations.

caption.1: Turn the dial to aim the switch. From the wiring alone, see which earlier switches could flip it. Then show a real sentence: which ones actually did?
caption.2: The weights-only pullback ranks every upstream latent before you read any text. Multiply by those latents' activations on a sentence to see what really drove it.
caption.3: Toy 2-D directions: pullback pᵢ = cosine of the angle between the reading and decoder directions; input-dependent influence = pᵢ·aᵢ. Real directions span the full residual width.

where_else: Attribution graphs, which trace computation through transcoders instead of raw MLPs
Sparse autoencoders: the same machinery aimed at a layer's state instead of its function
Swapping any hard-to-read subroutine for a readable approximation you can test
Weights-first analysis: form a theory from the wiring, then check it on data

hamming.what: An SAE-shaped model that learns to produce an MLP layer's output from its input through a sparse layer of readable latents.
hamming.when: When your circuit passes through MLP layers, or you want a latent's causes from the weights before looking at text.
hamming.why: It replaces a sealed, superposed computation with sparse switches whose wiring you can trace upstream, which is what attribution graphs are built on.

object.title: The folded landscape
object.subtitle: One output of an MLP over a 2-D slice of its input, rebuilt from a few switch-ramps plus a small leftover.

cap.1: The sealed machine's output over a slice of its inputs: a landscape with folds and faint ripples.
cap.2: One output direction of a real MLP layer, plotted over a 2-D slice of its input space (toy).
cap.3: A projection of mlp_out onto one direction as a function of a 2-D input slice; illustrative, not GPT-2's actual layer.

cap.1: One switch alone: flat on one side of a line, a ramp rising on the other. That ramp is one latent's part.
cap.2: A latent contributes ReLU(w·x + b) times its decoder vector: zero until the input crosses its line, then linear.
cap.3: Each latent's contribution along an output direction is a ReLU ramp over a half-space: w_encᵢ defines the fold, W_decᵢ the slope.

cap.1: Two switches, two folds. Each one only matters where it is switched on.
cap.2: The output is the sum of the active latents' parts; inactive latents contribute exactly nothing.
cap.3: Superposing sparse ReLU ramps gives a piecewise-linear map; sparsity means few ramps are active at any input.

cap.1: Three switches rebuild the landscape almost exactly. What is missing are the faint ripples.
cap.2: The transcoder's approximation: good but not perfect. The gap is the error term.
cap.3: mlp_out ≈ W_dec f + b_dec; the residual mlp_out − transcoder output is what use_error_term adds back.

cap.1: Add the ripples back and you have the real machine again. That is what keeping the error term means.
cap.2: use_error_term=True: the model runs unchanged while you read the latents; False: it runs on the transcoder alone.
cap.3: With the error term, analysis is exact and latents explain the non-error part; without it, conclusions hold only as far as the replacement is faithful.

cap.1: From above, each fold line is where one switch turns on. You can point at any spot and name which switches are lit.
cap.2: Reading a region = listing the active latents there: that is what makes the layer's function interpretable.
cap.3: Fold lines partition input space into regions with fixed active sets, so the computation is locally a sum of a few named terms.

options.t: The MLP's output, from the MLP's input

predict.why: An SAE reconstructs an activation; a transcoder maps the MLP's input to its output, replacing the computation.
